# Cerefox Decision Log — 2026 Q2 (Part 4)

> Continuation of "Cerefox Decision Log — 2026 Q2 (Part 3)". Part 3 hit
> 55,370 characters with the 2026-05-27 v0.5.3 paths-precedence-inversion
> entry, exceeding the ~50,000-character split threshold. Per the rule
> in `CLAUDE.md` ("finish the current entry, then start a new document"),
> v0.5.3 closed Part 3 and Part 4 opens here with v0.5.4.
>
> Splitting policy: when an entry would push a Decision Log document past
> ~50,000 characters, the next entry starts a new document. Search all
> parts via `cerefox_search` query `"Cerefox Decision Log"`.
>
> Entries are in **reverse chronological order** — latest at the top.

---

## What belongs in this log

(Same rules as Parts 1+2+3, repeated here so this document stands alone for new readers.)

This log captures **decisions, tradeoffs, and lessons learned** — not implementation details.

**Include**: architectural decisions with rationale, design tradeoffs (we considered X vs Y, chose Y because Z), failures and what we learned from them, platform gotchas and workarounds, principles and guardrails with their reasoning, **maintainer-only operational rituals that don't belong in the OSS docs** (npm publish bootstrap, supabase deploy credentials, etc.).

**Do not include**: feature descriptions (that's CHANGELOG), implementation details (that's commits), operational changes, documentation updates, **specific bug fixes** (those belong in git history and on GitHub issues). If the entry could be a commit message or a ticket title, it probably doesn't belong here.

**Format**: each entry has a date, a short title, Context (why this came up), Decision or Lesson (what we chose and why), and optionally an Outcome or Rationale.

---

## 2026-05-27 — v0.6 pre-kickoff design pass + test plan rename (process meta-entry)

**Context**: v0.5.4 shipped 2026-05-27 evening. Before kicking off iter-24
(v0.6 "TS Web Server", FastAPI → Hono), we held a thorough pre-kickoff
design pass that produced a locked-decisions table in `docs/plan.md`
§ Iteration 24. The pattern is new — earlier iterations had headline
items but skipped the locked-decisions-up-front discipline. v0.6 is the
largest port we'll do (35 endpoints + frontend bundling + zod schemas +
configure-agent Phase 2), so investing the design pass upfront makes
the implementation atomic.

This is a **process meta-entry**, not a closing entry. The proper "v0.6
closing decisions" entry will land in Part 4 (or Part 5 if size threshold
hits) when iter-24 ships — distinct from this one. Captured now so the
fresh-session pickup that starts iter-24 has the meta-context.

### 1. Test plan renamed: `v0.5-manual-test-plan.md` → `v0.7-manual-test-plan.md`

The doc always tracked the v0.5 → v0.7 strangler-fig arc; the v0.5-prefixed
name expired the moment v0.5.1 shipped. Renamed via `git mv` (PR #54) so
history is preserved — `git log --follow` traces back to the v0.5.0 cut.
The renamed file's intro section explicitly explains the rename and
documents the rolling-scope pattern (iter-24 adds a v0.6 section, iter-25
adds a v0.7 section, both ticked at each cut).

**Note for future readers**: §4 of the v0.5.4 entry below and §4 of the
v0.5.0 entry in Part 3 still reference the **old** filename
(`v0.5-manual-test-plan.md`). Those references are preserved **verbatim**
per the "keep entries verbatim" rule in CLAUDE.md — Decision Log entries
are snapshots of decisions at the time they were made; we don't rewrite
history. Readers following the broken link land on the renamed file via
git's `--follow` semantics or via the intro of the new file, which
explains the rename.

### 2. Pre-kickoff design pass — process pattern worth keeping

For the first time, the maintainer and I held a structured design pass
BEFORE iteration kickoff:

1. **Investigation**: read the design doc + plan.md headlines together,
   counted the actual surface (35 endpoints, not 30+; frontend bundling
   gap; 3 ingestion endpoints depend on the v0.7 pipeline).
2. **Surface the high-impact questions**: 4 decisions whose answers
   materially change the design (ingestion scope, schema deploy timing,
   parity test approach, iteration size).
3. **Lock answers in a "Locked design decisions" table** in plan.md so
   later sessions inherit the rationale.
4. **Review pass**: 5 doc inconsistencies caught + 9 known-risks
   tabulated (R1–R9) with default plans + the Part where each resolves.
5. **Second review round**: surfaced two reversals (see §3 below).
6. Produced a "fresh-session pickup" pointer block at the end of the
   iter-24 plan section.

Two PRs produced this pass: **PR #54** (original design pass) +
**PR #55** (review-pass fixes + simplifications). Both docs-only.
No code; pure thinking.

**General rule (worth keeping)**: for any iteration whose size is **L
or larger** (T-shirt), hold a pre-kickoff design pass that produces a
locked-decisions table in plan.md. Cost: hours of conversation + a
docs-only PR. Value: catches design reversals early (paying with
thinking instead of with re-implementation), captures rationale for
fresh-session pickups, produces a self-contained design that the
iteration's actual implementation PR can reference instead of
re-deriving.

### 3. Two reversals during the design pass — value of multiple rounds

Both reversals happened in the design pass, BEFORE any code was written:

**Reversal A — "v0.6 internal milestone" → "v0.6 normal release"**.
We briefly considered tagging v0.6 in git but skipping the GH Release
+ npm publish, on the grounds that 3 ingestion endpoints returning 503
made it "not really ready". Reversed within the same design pass when
we worked through the implementation complexity: a `--tag-only` flag
on `cut_release.ts`, source-vs-npm UX divergence during the build,
migration-v0.5.md gymnastics ("users skip v0.6"), and the contributor
confusion of "pull main, see TS web with 503s — is this broken or
expected?" The friendly 503 toast UX with a working CLI fallback
(`cerefox ingest file.md` uses the EF and works fully) is good enough.
v0.6 ships as a normal release.

**Reversal B — "Python web deprecation banner in v0.6" → "deferred to
v0.7"**. We briefly planned to land the banner in v0.6 alongside the
TS web. Maintainer pushed back: "we can't block users from using the
Python web until the full app is fully tested." Banner timing now tied
to TS-web-functional-completeness: lands in v0.7 Part 25L at the same
moment the 503 stubs swap to in-process pipeline calls.

**General rule (worth keeping)**: every design pass should have at
least two review rounds. The first one surfaces the architecture
questions; the second one challenges the answers. Most of the value
comes from the second round — that's where briefly-held decisions
get caught and reversed before they become code.

### 4. T-shirt sizing replaces week estimates

Earlier iterations used "~4 weeks part-time" / "~6 weeks part-time" /
etc. The maintainer pointed out (rightly) that all v0.4 → v0.5.4
iterations took at most **a couple of hours of AI-paired session
time**, so human-developer week estimates were misleading by 1-2
orders of magnitude.

**New convention**: T-shirt sizes only.

| Size | Examples |
|---|---|
| S | v0.5.1 (drop one bin), small doc PRs |
| M | v0.5.2, v0.5.3, v0.5.4 (each one hotfix + docs + Decision Log entry) |
| L | (none yet — would be a multi-Part patch release without a major surface change) |
| **XL** | **iter-24 (v0.6 TS web — 35 endpoints + frontend + Phase 2 configure-agent)**, **iter-25 (v0.7 TS ingestion — chunking parity is delicate, scripts/*.py ports too)** |
| XXL | (none planned — would be a multi-iteration restructure) |

Where T-shirt sizes appear: plan.md iteration headers, design doc §13
per-iteration entries. Where they DO NOT appear: Decision Log entries
(those are about what was decided, not how long it took).

### 5. Other locked decisions worth surfacing here

The full list lives in plan.md § Iteration 24 "Locked design decisions"
table. Highlights worth keeping in Decision Log because they reflect
architectural patterns, not iter-24-specific scope:

- **Zod schemas in `_shared/schemas/` as the response-shape contract**,
  consumed by both server and frontend. Runtime `.parse()` enforcement
  in dev mode (`NODE_ENV !== 'production'`), skip in production.
  Narrow byte-snapshot tests for ~5 critical endpoints — matches the
  v0.4.0 Decision Log §6 rule ("byte-snapshot only where shape really
  matters").
- **Configure-agent `ConfigWriter` interface extended** to support both
  `direct-write` (JSON file) and `delegated` (shell out to target
  client's CLI) kinds. Adding Cursor/Codex/Gemini in v0.6 picks the
  appropriate kind per client. Codex specifically needs TOML support
  (`smol-toml` or `@iarna/toml` dep) — risk R1 in the iter-24 table.
- **No TS port of the e2e suite**. Python `pytest -m e2e` already
  covers Supabase end-to-end against the live DB; duplicating in TS
  just to skip-in-CI is wasted effort. The Python suite is
  server-implementation-agnostic at the `/api/v1/*` HTTP boundary, so
  it can be pointed at the TS server during the iter-24 manual test
  plan walk.

### Cross-references

- Iter-24 design + 12 Parts + locked decisions + R1–R9 risks: `docs/plan.md`
  § Iteration 24.
- Iter-25 (v0.7) headlines: `docs/plan.md` § Iteration 25.
- Design doc abstract framing: `docs/specs/polish-and-distribution-design.md`
  §13 v0.6.0 + §13 v0.7.0.
- PRs that produced this design pass: **#54** + **#55** (both
  docs-only, merged into main).
- Test plan: `docs/research/v0.7-manual-test-plan.md` (renamed from
  `v0.5-manual-test-plan.md` in PR #54).
- v0.5.4 closing entry: below in this document.

### Revisit triggers

- (a) When iter-24 closes (v0.6 ships): write the proper "v0.6 closing
  decisions" entry in Part 4 (or Part 5 if size threshold hits).
  Distinct from this pre-kickoff entry — that one covers what shipped
  + lessons learned during the build, this one covers the design
  process itself.
- (b) If a future L+ iteration skips the pre-kickoff design pass and
  surfaces avoidable reversals during implementation: re-read §2 +
  §3 of this entry. The pattern's cost is small; the value is
  non-linear for big migrations.
- (c) If T-shirt sizing turns out to be too coarse (e.g., XL covers
  too wide a range): add SM/ML/XXL granularity. Don't reintroduce
  hour/week estimates — those are misleading at AI-paired pace.

## 2026-05-27 — v0.5.4: configure-agent claude-code writer fix + the missing round-trip test

**Context**: surfaced live during the maintainer's v0.5.3 upgrade test on
2026-05-27 evening. After `cerefox configure-agent --tool claude-code`
reported success (`✓ Claude Code configured`, `config: /Users/fotis/.claude/mcp.json`,
`action: created`), the maintainer started a fresh Claude Code session and
**none of the Cerefox MCP tools appeared**. Root cause: the writer was
writing to the wrong file — Claude Code reads user-scope MCP servers from
`~/.claude.json` (a dot-file in `$HOME`) under the `.mcpServers` key, not
from `~/.claude/mcp.json` (under the `.claude` directory). Doctor was
silently lying about the same path. The bug had shipped to npm in every
v0.5.x release (v0.5.0 through v0.5.3).

### 1. The bug — and why it was visible to literally no automated test

`packages/memory/src/cli/util/mcp-config-writers.ts` (v0.5.0–v0.5.3) had:

```ts
function claudeCodeConfigPath(): string {
  return join(homedir(), ".claude", "mcp.json");
}
```

That path doesn't exist in Claude Code's read list. Claude Code's actual
locations:
- **User scope**: `~/.claude.json` → `.mcpServers.<name>`
- **Project scope**: `<cwd>/.mcp.json` → `.mcpServers.<name>`

The `~/.claude/` directory IS a Claude Code path — but it's for caches,
history, and plugin data, not for MCP servers. Our writer mistook a
plausible-looking dir for the server config location.

The `lifecycle-commands.test.ts` tests passed in CI for every v0.5.x
release. Why? They used `--config-path <tmpFile>` to redirect the writer
away from the real `~/.claude/mcp.json` to a tmpfile, then asserted the
tmpfile got valid JSON. **The tests verified the file-write code path
was correct in isolation; they never verified the file lands somewhere
Claude Code actually reads from.**

Doctor compounded the lie: `checkMcpConfigs()` scanned `~/.claude/mcp.json`
for *any* file presence (not for cerefox content), so doctor reported
"Claude Code (user)" green when the writer's broken output was on disk.
Two surfaces consistently wrong → user trusts the green check → bug
ships.

### 2. The fix — delegate, don't direct-write

Two options were on the table:

**(A) Direct-write to `~/.claude.json` with deep merge.** Read the
existing 48KB JSON, add `.mcpServers.cerefox`, write back with backup.

**(B) Shell out to `claude mcp add cerefox --scope user --`.** Let Claude
Code's own CLI manage its own config.

Decision: **B**. Reasoning:

- **Future-proof**: if Claude Code changes its config schema or storage
  location in a future version, our writer breaks. Their CLI tracks
  their schema; delegating insulates us.
- **Lower risk**: `~/.claude.json` is a 48 KB file with dozens of keys
  (`oauthAccount`, `projects`, `cachedGrowthBookFeatures`, …). A bug in
  our deep-merge code could corrupt the maintainer's entire Claude Code
  state. Delegating means Claude Code does the merge with its own
  battle-tested code.
- **Self-documenting**: `claude mcp add` is the recipe in
  `connect-agents.md`. Our writer doing the same thing under the hood
  matches the manual-config guidance — fewer "wait, why doesn't this
  match the docs" moments.
- **Honest configPath**: post-write we report
  `config: ~/.claude.json (managed by claude mcp add)`. Even if Claude
  Code internally writes to a different file in a future version, the
  report stays accurate (we report the canonical path; the delegated
  CLI handles the implementation).

The escape hatch: `--config-path FILE` still triggers direct-write mode
(even for delegated writers like claude-code). Preserves the v0.5.0–v0.5.3
test path AND gives power users an escape if they want a specific file
location.

**Architectural addition**: `ConfigWriter` interface gains a
`kind: "direct-write" | "delegated"` field. Direct-write for clients
without a CLI helper (Claude Desktop). Delegated for clients with one
(Claude Code). Adding Cursor / Codex / Gemini in v0.5.x or v0.6 will
pick the appropriate kind.

### 3. Defensive backup — applied even when we don't write the file

Even though Claude Code's own CLI writes `~/.claude.json`, our writer
takes a `~/.claude.json.pre-cerefox.bak` snapshot BEFORE invoking
`claude mcp add`. Reasoning:

- If `claude mcp add` errors mid-write, the file could be partially
  modified. A pre-cerefox snapshot lets the user `mv` it back.
- The Claude Code CLI's own behavior is opaque to us — it might rewrite
  the entire file with formatting changes, not just append the new
  entry. The backup preserves the user's exact byte content.
- Cost: ~50KB on disk, ~10ms wallclock. Negligible.

**General rule (worth keeping)**: when shelling out to a third-party
CLI that modifies a user-managed file, snapshot the file first. The
cost is trivial; the recovery option is invaluable when the third-
party CLI does something unexpected.

### 4. The missing test: "spawn the client and verify tools appear"

The real failure here wasn't the path mistake (which was a small bug
in a single function). It was that **no test in CI ever spawned Claude
Code and asked it whether the cerefox tools were visible**. The whole
point of `configure-agent` is to wire up a third-party client. A test
that doesn't verify that wiring landed is testing the wrong thing.

Why didn't we have such a test?

- **Claude Code isn't installed in CI**. Running it would require either
  bundling the `claude` binary in the GitHub Actions runner (heavy) or
  skipping the test in CI (which defeats the purpose).
- **The test runs against the maintainer's machine only**. Live e2e is
  what we have for Supabase + OpenAI checks (the `LIVE_OK` probe). It
  works because the maintainer's `.env` is on disk, the network is up,
  and a real query returns real data.
- **For MCP clients, there's no equivalent "machine has it"**. We
  detected Supabase availability with a 200 OK probe; the parallel
  for Claude Code would be "spawn `claude` and parse `claude mcp list`
  output". Doable but more work.

**Decision (v0.5.4)**: add a post-write smoke test that runs `claude mcp list`
and asserts `cerefox` is in the output. **Gated on `command -v claude`**
(skip if not installed, same probe pattern as the LIVE_OK gate). On
the maintainer's machine + any contributor's machine with Claude Code
installed, the test runs. In CI without Claude Code, the test skips.

Deferred to a follow-up patch because v0.5.4 is already large; the test
needs careful sandboxing (running real `claude mcp add` would pollute
the contributor's actual `~/.claude.json`). Tracked.

**General rule (worth keeping)**: **whenever you write code that
configures a third-party tool, your test plan must include "spawn the
third-party tool and verify it reads what you wrote".** A test that
asserts "we produced bytes" isn't a test of integration; it's a test
of byte production. The real contract is "the third-party tool behaves
correctly after we configure it" — that's what the test must check.
Even probe-and-skip is better than nothing.

### 5. The pattern of "review surface vs lived surface"

This bug surfaced a process gap. Multiple eyes on the v0.5.0 PR (#47):
maintainer + me + CI + iter-23 plan review. None of us spotted the
wrong path. Why?

- **Plausibility**: `~/.claude/mcp.json` *looks* right. Claude Code does
  have a `~/.claude/` directory. The path passes a casual eye-check.
- **Test coverage was a false signal**: green CI on `configure-agent`
  tests reads as "the writer works". It only tests "bytes are produced
  correctly", not "the right tool reads them".
- **The bug doesn't manifest on the dev's machine**: the maintainer who
  reviewed the PR didn't *use* configure-agent on their own machine until
  v0.5.3 — their existing Claude Desktop config from before v0.4.0 was
  still working (Python soft-wrapper path). The bug only fires when the
  user actually runs the command AND starts a fresh Claude Code session.

The fix for this class of bug is **lived testing**, not more code review.
The v0.5 manual test plan (`docs/research/v0.5-manual-test-plan.md`,
documented as decision #4 in the v0.5.0 Decision Log entry) is the right
tool. It has a "configure-agent claude-code" line item; the maintainer
ticked it without spawning a fresh Claude Code session to verify tools
appeared. **Update the test plan to require the spawn step.**

**General rule (worth keeping)**: every "configure tool X" command in
the test plan must end with "spawn X in a fresh process and verify the
configuration took effect". A green checkbox without the spawn step is
half-tested.

### 6. Why this is a hotfix (v0.5.4), not a minor

v0.5.0 is the npm-CLI release; configure-agent is a flagship command.
Shipping it broken to npm for four consecutive releases (v0.5.0, v0.5.1,
v0.5.2, v0.5.3) is a real UX hazard for anyone testing v0.5.x. Hotfix
priority same as v0.5.2 (soft-wrapper recursion).

Patches go to npm by the same flow (cut_release.ts + release.yml).
Affected users (anyone who ran `configure-agent --tool claude-code`
on v0.5.0–v0.5.3): documented in CHANGELOG and migration-v0.5.md with
the exact remediation. Orphan `~/.claude/mcp.json` files left by the
buggy versions are inert — Claude Code never read them — but doctor
in v0.5.4 still scans only the *correct* path, so the orphan stays
invisible. Users can delete it manually (`rm ~/.claude/mcp.json`); we
don't touch it because (a) we wrote it, (b) deleting files we wrote
without explicit user consent feels invasive, and (c) it does no harm.

### Cross-references

- v0.5.3 paths-precedence-inversion entry: Part 3, 2026-05-27 entry
  ("Bringing the v1.0 `.env` flip forward by ~10 minors").
- v0.5.2 soft-wrapper recursion entry: Part 3, 2026-05-27 entry.
- Writer implementation: `packages/memory/src/cli/util/mcp-config-writers.ts`
  v0.5.4 (delegated kind + `claude mcp add --scope user`).
- Doctor fix: `packages/memory/src/cli/util/checks.ts::checkMcpConfigs`
  reads `~/.claude.json`'s `.mcpServers.cerefox`.
- Migration guide section: `docs/guides/migration-v0.5.md` § "v0.5.4
  fixed cerefox configure-agent --tool claude-code".
- v0.5 manual test plan update (pending): add "spawn a fresh Claude
  Code session and verify cerefox tools appear" to the configure-agent
  line item.

### Revisit triggers

- (a) When Cursor / Codex / Gemini support lands: pick `kind: delegated`
  for any client that has a CLI helper for MCP config management.
  Direct-write only for clients that genuinely don't have one.
- (b) When the deferred "spawn-and-verify" smoke test lands: this entry's
  §4 stops being a follow-up and becomes a "shipped" line item.
- (c) If Claude Code ever moves its user-scope MCP config out of
  `~/.claude.json`: our delegated writer keeps working (Claude Code's
  CLI tracks the move). Doctor's check needs updating; that's the
  signal to revisit.
- (d) If `claude mcp add --scope user` is renamed or changes its
  invocation: the writer breaks loudly (non-zero exit from spawnSync).
  Recovery: bump to a v0.5.x patch that updates `claudeCodeDelegated()`.
  Mitigation: pin the `claude` CLI major version requirement somewhere
  (probably `cerefox doctor`).

---

## Notes for future Part 4 entries

Part 4 starts fresh. Expected entries between now and next split:

- v0.6: web/API ported to TS. Likely a multi-entry build closing the
  Python web server. Decision Log entry on the migration strategy.
- v0.7: ingestion pipeline ported. Likely multi-entry, schema-deploy
  port discussion (does CEREFOX_DATABASE_URL go through the TS CLI?).
- Various v0.5.x patches as the strangler-fig surfaces hidden corners.

When this part crosses ~50,000 chars, the next entry starts Part 5 —
same rule as Parts 2 → 3 and Parts 3 → 4.
